facts.title: Named After an Asteroid
facts.text: English chemist William Hyde Wollaston discovered palladium in 1802 while studying crude platinum ore dissolved in aqua regia. He named it after Pallas, a large asteroid spotted just a year earlier in 1802 by astronomer Heinrich Olbers. The asteroid itself was named for Pallas Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom and warfare.

facts.title: Sold by Anonymous Handbill
facts.text: Rather than announce his find through the scientific establishment, Wollaston secretly sold palladium as a 'new silver' through a London shop in 1803 via anonymous leaflets. A skeptical chemist, Richard Chenevix, publicly declared it was merely a platinum-mercury alloy, sparking a famous dispute. Wollaston eventually revealed himself as the discoverer in 1805, vindicating the metal as a genuine new element.

facts.title: A Metallic Sponge for Hydrogen
facts.text: Palladium has an extraordinary appetite for hydrogen: at room temperature it can absorb up to about 900 times its own volume of hydrogen gas. The hydrogen atoms slip into the spaces of palladium's crystal lattice, making it function like a chemical sponge. This property makes palladium invaluable for hydrogen purification and storage research.

facts.title: The Catalytic Converter Workhorse
facts.text: More than three-quarters of all palladium mined goes into catalytic converters in cars. There it speeds up reactions that turn toxic carbon monoxide, unburned hydrocarbons, and nitrogen oxides into less harmful carbon dioxide, water, and nitrogen. Its rising use in gasoline engines once pushed palladium's price above that of gold.

facts.title: Nobel-Winning Chemistry
facts.text: Palladium is the heart of cross-coupling reactions that let chemists stitch carbon atoms together with precision. Richard Heck, Ei-ichi Negishi, and Akira Suzuki shared the 2010 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing these palladium-catalyzed methods. The reactions are now essential for making pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and electronic materials.

facts.title: Forged in Colliding Stars
facts.text: Palladium is one of the heavy elements thought to form mainly through the rapid neutron-capture process, or r-process. This requires extreme environments such as the merging of two neutron stars, like the event detected by gravitational waves in 2017. The palladium on Earth is essentially stardust from such ancient cosmic catastrophes.

facts.title: Mined Mostly in Two Places
facts.text: Russia and South Africa together supply the vast majority of the world's palladium. Much of it comes not from dedicated mines but as a byproduct of nickel and platinum mining, such as Russia's Norilsk deposits in Siberia. This concentrated supply makes the metal's price unusually sensitive to geopolitics and labor disruptions.

facts.title: The Lightest Platinum-Group Metal
facts.text: With a density of about 12 grams per cubic centimeter and a melting point near 1,555 degrees Celsius, palladium is the lightest and lowest-melting of the six platinum-group metals. It is also remarkably resistant to corrosion and tarnish in ordinary air. These traits make it useful in dentistry, jewelry, and reliable electrical contacts.

facts.title: Secret Inside Your Electronics
facts.text: Tiny amounts of palladium hide inside billions of multilayer ceramic capacitors found in phones, laptops, and other devices. The metal forms the thin internal electrodes that let these components store and release charge. Palladium is also used to plate connectors because it conducts well and stays corrosion-free.

facts.title: It Makes White Gold White
facts.text: Jewelers alloy palladium with gold to create some of the finest white gold, since palladium bleaches the yellow color while staying hypoallergenic. Pure palladium has also been recognized as a precious metal for jewelry, with British hallmarking beginning in 2010. Because it is naturally white, light, and never tarnishes, it appeals to people allergic to nickel.
